utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please look at document -- or, rather, Exhibit P36? My learned friend Zivanovic had questions for you concerning this document, and you commented upon the first part especially, which refers to the movement and composition of the armed groups on their way to Tuzla and Kladanj. What is your understanding of this section of the document? The way I understood you, and let me summarise it, this is some sort of a caution for the units out in the field to be aware of the dangers and threats lurking from them, if my understanding of your testimony and the document here is correct.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents which relate to tasks that are being issued to subordinated units contain information about the enemy, specifically when it comes to the implementation of combat assignments. What we have here is very specific information about the enemy, which points to the problems and the tasks that the individuals responsible have to carry out and they were specified in this document as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of the regulations you referred to, is there anything in this order that would run counter to the norms and regulations in force in Republika Srpska at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an obligation that was in accordance with all the regulations stipulating how the enemy is to be assessed and analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about this particular part of the document, wherein it is stated that, among the armed groups, criminals and villains can be found?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear on the basis of the document that specific caution is given to them in the situations requiring the disarming of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is just a caution and not an invitation to engage in lynching or retaliation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this is part of the task issued. The words "combat activity" is used and weapons. We know what this is all about, in combat. We know what happens to those who lay their arms down and what happens to those who continue engaging in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's listed as a question when it was really an answer. "And this is just a caution and not an invitation to engage in lynching or retaliation." I'm pretty sure that was an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a question. That was my question. That wasn't the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I heard the witness say that. Maybe I've been listening too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's been cleared. Now, thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Who is going next? I'm calling on the Beara team. Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuga.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Predrag Nikolic and I'm a lawyer for the Defence team of Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Let me put several questions to you concerning the security administration, in view of the fact that Mr. Beara himself discharged certain duties in that sector. In the system of the organisation of the VRS, the security administration was an organ of the Main Staff, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: By virtue of its position it was the highest professional organ of the VRS in terms of the professional management of security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was its role and task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can this role be summarised down to the main functions: Counter-intelligence activities, professional management of security organs and of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are its basic functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As an organ of the Main Staff, the commander of the Main Staff is the one who directly commands over the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff commands directly over the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So he is under the command of the Main Staff commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We said that the security administration was the highest professional organ managing subordinate security organs. Am I right in saying that in -- the security administration performs this role of its, through instructions and directions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 93 of the rules of service stipulates that the administration or, rather, the administration chief is the one who shall interpret the rules of service and provide more detailed instructions, which means that that is its function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In view of the nature of the instructions and explanations, can these enactments coming from the security administration be regarded as administrative enactments?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not command enactments, they do not fall within the field of commands, but they are binding instructions to those who fall within that professional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So they are not commanding enactments, but they are binding in terms of professional management?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are binding so far as they relate to the issues with which an individual has to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professional management also encompasses the professional management of the military police, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional management mentioned herein also encompasses the professional management of the military police of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In what way is the professional management of the military police of the Main Staff exercised?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional management of the military police of the Main Staff is exercised through a certain organ of the security administration who deals with the military police affairs. He, in turn, is under the command of the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about this professional control, am I correct if I were to say that the security administration achieves this by planning and through authorised bearers, performs the supply of the military police by -- with weaponry, equipment, drafting the training plan, and the programme of combat training?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration is the tactical bearer of equipping military police and the professional cadre, in terms of training. It organises and resolves other questions except deciding on the use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is the moment to return to a question which was put by my colleague, Ms. Nikolic, regarding the use of military police, and I conclude from your testimony that the security organ never can order the use of military police but can only suggest or propose certain measures to the commander.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs, in relation to the military police, does not have the right to order and issue assignments. They don't have the right of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the military police unit that is attached to the Main Staff, then we have in mind the unit that was part of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a military police unit of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska which was part of the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was one of the assignments and the subject of the work of the security organs also cooperation with the civilian authority organs, specifically the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These questions are regulated by regulations, and particularly in Republika Srpska this sphere has been specified in more detail through special documents and instructions of the President of Republika Srpska, between the Main Staff and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, this cooperation cannot proceed directly between the subordinate organs of the MUP and the security administration, but only through the Main Staff and the appropriate staff within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are certain questions that can be dealt with directly in cooperation with certain structures of the Ministry of the Interior, but these things are resolved pursuant to regulations on mutual cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now to clarify the meaning of two terms, the terms of "prisoners" and the term "detainees." Please, can you, based on your long years of work in that area, can you define these two terms?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "prisoners" is defined by regulations on the application of rules of international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions of 1949. These are members of enemy forces who have the status of prisoners of war and who are under the authority of the force that captured them. They have been disarmed and have stopped putting up resistance. As for detainees, these are persons who have the status under the law on criminal procedure and in relation to them, they are treated in the manner prescribed by the law on criminal procedure. If we are talking about prior criminal proceedings, these persons could be detained, they could be taken into custody, and be treated pursuant to the appropriate regulations of the organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about prisoners, in your practice of many years, have you ever heard of the term "live tongue"? And if you have heard this term, "zivi jezik," can you explain its meaning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "zivi jezik" has been used for a long time as -- well, in terms of its meaning or as a concept, implying that it's a bearer of certain information who is in the position of being able to speak of them, to tell them. That would indicate that. But it's used more in jargon. It's not something that is an official term that would define a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a colloquial expression and as you said yourself, it refers to a person belonging to the prisoners of war category or group.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to define it as precisely as that because "zivi jezik," live tongue, is not a completely defined term so I could not take that to mean a member of the prisoner of war group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we define that as a person from whom the security organ receives useful or necessary information from the aspect of counter-intelligence or intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In replying to this question of yours, I would rule out the term "zivi jezik," live source of information, because it's not a clear definition in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us come back then, to the area of responsibilities of the security organ within the Main Staff. We talked about instructions, directives. Does the security administration, through its organs, and in immediate contacts out in the field, perform its function?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration is the one that assesses the form and the manner of implementation it would apply in a given situation for the purposes of professional control and so that the expert instructions and requirements are implemented. Therefore, going out into the field, direct influence and everything else would be a method of the operation of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So this calls for the security administration to be in constant contact throughout the whole territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration has jurisdiction over the entire territory of the Army of Republika Srpska and where this army is carrying out its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As part of the implementation of these assignments, the security organs are using certain methods and means. Please, would I be correct if I were to say that when using methods, the commander of the unit is the one who makes a decision on this? He's the sole person making this decision? But if means are used, this gives the possibility that the security organ decides for itself about the means?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a crucial difference here. By applying methods of work, in the work of security organs, this is done pursuant to the rules on methods of work. There are four methods of work that the security organ applies independently and without any special authorisation. As for the rest, they only are applied once they are proposed and on the basis of received authorisation from the authorised senior officer who was in the Army of Republika Srpska -- actually, in the Army of Republika Srpska, he would be the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. As for the means, operative technical means, of the security organs, their application is authorised as part of the methods of work that those means are planned for. So I apologise, there is a difference there between applying the methods, which methods, and the application of operative and technical means within those given methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Vuga, based on your long years of experience and the analysis which you made in reference to the functioning of the security organs in Republika Srpska, would I be correct if I were to say that based on all that was said, it can be concluded that there isn't and there does not exist a parallel system of control in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this question, I'm going to answer in accordance with the explanations that I provided earlier, and that is professional control is set up along the vertical line, such as -- the same as command. It's a vertical line. However, command was a single thing executed along the line of command, and command is based on singleness of command. There cannot be parallel command. This would then interfere and disrupt the system of command, if such a case were to exist. Professional control is set up along the vertical line whereby the security organ of the superior command in the professional sense would control the security organ in the subordinate command. It's not a question of a parallel chain of authority, power and command, but about professional linkage into a functional whole in order for information to flow, the information is specific, and in order to issue directives that are not commands or orders but they are to a sufficient degree requests for the army to be protected, in terms of counter-intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. After reconsideration, we decided not to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau is not cross-examining. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's been an hour and a half since the last break. Should we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. By all means. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one thing. My guess is Mr. Haynes will take the rest of the time but perhaps if he doesn't, could I ask that the cross-examination start on Monday, just -- this is radically, my cross-examination, radically faster than we had expected and my guess is there won't be much time anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to commit myself first and my colleagues either before hearing Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can't promise that I'll fill the day. I'll take a little while. I think we were all a little taken aback by the speed of Ms. Nikolic's cross-examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will come back to you later on, Mr. McCloskey. --- Break taken at 12.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, Mr. Vuga.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic, and after that, I think you'll be free to enjoy your weekend. I don't think I'm going to be very long but bear with me and it will be over for today, I think. I'd like to start by going back to the beginning of your evidence. You retired from military service in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I couldn't discern this from your curriculum vitae, do you remember precisely what month it was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My active service in the army of Yugoslavia stopped on the 30th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the last period of your active service, you were engaged in the education of security officers; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last period of my service, I was the assistant chief of the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The security service within the army of Yugoslavia was comprised of specially trained and qualified operatives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's quite literally at all levels, not just the security organs themselves, but members of the security organs and the military police received special training to work in those particular areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in order to achieve advancement within the security service, you had to, as it were, put in the time and pass the exams?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were involved in training, yourself, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that training of military policemen and security operatives at every level?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a separate education for the military policemen and it was separate from the military operatives, but not at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And part of the training and the qualification process, did that involve an understanding and a knowledge of the rules of service and the rules that related to the security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of the compulsory curriculum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've read an awful lot of material in preparing your report, but has your research led you to discover how many professional or trained security officers there were in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My research was based on the analysis of combat preparedness in 1995 -- 4, that we have discussed during my testimony. It says in those documents that 50 per cent of the security organ members in the Zvornik Brigade were fully trained in equipment and that the remaining 50 per cent were being trained on the job in the Zvornik Brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in terms of the appropriate level of seniority and qualification for the position of chief of security within a brigade, did you ever, within the JNA, come across a second lieutenant holding that office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the JNA and appointment in the JNA is much too broad an issue for me to be able to give you a precise answer. In principle, there were no such cases, unless those were something that went beyond the prescribed principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you discovered what training and qualification of security officers was taking place within the Army of Republika Srpska generally, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any documents that would help me drive at a conclusion, and I did not dwell upon that issue because that issue was not a specific part of my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's very fair of you to say so and I'll take that no further. At the conclusion of your cross-examination by Mr. Peter Nikolic just now, you were asked about the existence of parallel chains of command. You gave a very long answer and I'm going to put this to you: Isn't it the case that the question of what authority unit commanders had to give orders to security organs was a very difficult problem even within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the JNA, this was a much lesser problem, if this is what we are talking about. I did my research within that area and my conclusion would be somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you to look at a document now I don't think you have seen before. And I don't have a hard copy binder for you so you're going to have to look at the screen, Mr. Vuga, I'm sorry. It's 7D483, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If counsel has any more documents that he intends to use, I don't believe we received any notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I believe you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is normally right but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a spare copy that can be handed over?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe it's ever been printed but I think it can be transmitted very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't need to delay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see that document, Mr. Vuga?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to read it through in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet, but I'm working on it. I'm trying to look at the entirety of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, let me know when you've done that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the document, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the document is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an order sent to the unit commanders, but it refers to the command of the 17th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In which army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no signature but I believe it is clear that the 17th Corps was part of the JNA. Now I have the signature. The commander of the 17th Corps is what is indicated on the stamp, and this is indeed the JNA in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And would you agree that, as it were, that the basis of that document is very similar to the instruction of October 1995 that we saw relating to the Army of Republika Srpska, namely, that unit commanders are being reminded of their authority in relation to security organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a similarity, but I have to go back in providing my answer so as to make you understand what I'm talking about. This is 1999, ^ the month of February, and it says here, as of lately. And I was with the JNA between 1956 and 1992, for 36 years in total. My answer cannot be based on the document dating back to the month of February, to the moment when I left the army. The period is far too short for me to arrive at a -- at any conclusions about such a long period during which these occurrences had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I see. But you will have seen many such orders, and I want your assistance, really, with the second paragraph and the first sentence of it. It reads, in English, "Unit commanders are not authorised for the KO tasks of the security organs." How do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I've already tackled that in my previous answers and provided sufficient explanation. This means that by applying methods of work, in keeping with the guidelines, this is what the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is -- approves, and in this case this was the Federal Secretary for National Defence or a person authorised by them. Nobody else has the right to decide upon his decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So is that another way of saying that there was a large area of the work of the security organs in which they were autonomous?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was room strictly provided for by the rules, and in that area, there was absolute control. Independence was only in the part where you were supposed to find the most adequate source of information and to apply the adequate methods. Everything else was under the strict control of the professional organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you would agree with that document, would you, that in that area, the unit commanders had no authority? That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to agree with the document. The document is what it is and it is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you retired, your boss in the JNA would have been the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My boss, at the moment when I retired, was the chief of the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who answered to the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He answered to the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was quite unlike the chiefs of all the other organs in the Yugoslav National Army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not dwell upon the issue of other organs answering and to whom, but I know how I answered to and to whom. I answered to my chief within his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but you've come here to give evidence as an expert about, as it were, the structure of the security service within the JNA and the VRS. What I'm putting to you is that the security service in the JNA had a different boss to answer to to the rest of the Yugoslav National Army, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat your question? Because I'm not able to draw any conclusions as to what my answer may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Within the Main Staff of the JNA, there was a department for security and a department for intelligence; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Main Staff of the JNA, there was a department for security, which was, in professional terms, subordinated to the security administration. That existed in the General Staff rather than in the Main Staff. The name was the General Staff of the JNA, while I was a member of the JNA. And the security administration was an organ of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. It was an independent administration, and its chief was answerable for his work to the Federal Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doesn't seem to have covered the aspect of intelligence, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we come on to intelligence? Who did the intelligence department answer to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence administration was part of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So -- and that's, as it were, true of all the other organs of the army that we've seen, isn't it? The security department had ultimately a different head to the rest of the army; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the correct answer would lead us to the structure of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. What is missing is a very important concept of the armed forces of the Yugoslav army and what they consisted of. This is just one part thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on. I may come back to that. Of course, in the VRS, the security and intelligence services were united in the Main Staff for functional reasons; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska functioned in accordance with the conditions under which it was formed and the tasks that it was supposed to perform. So the intelligence and security functions followed that until the 13th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that meant, for example, in all units of the army, save for certain brigades and the Main Staff, there were separate sections for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 13th of January, 1995, onwards, and this is the relevant period for our considerations, the intelligence function as one of the very important operations functions was affiliated with the command staffs of those units where it was an integral part of the staff, whereas security was in the hands of the commander as the immediate superior officer to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we move on, please, to a document I know you've probably seen many times, but there are some questions you haven't been asked about it, and that's P2741, the instruction of October of 1994. Do you need to read it again, Mr. Vuga, or is it a document you're very familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document, but it will largely depend on your question whether I have to go in any depth because of the terminology and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Firstly, the preamble, the very first paragraph, "Lately, frequent problems, failures and irregularities have been registered in command and control over the security and intelligence organs at all levels." Did your researches lead to you discover what problems, failures and irregularities this document was referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have spoken about that in answering Mrs. Nikolic's questions. The problems that are stated herein are sufficiently big enough to prompt the issuance of this document. I did not research any other problems because they were within the Army of Republika Srpska in other units and at other levels different to those that I took into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably my fault, Mr. Vuga. What I meant to ask you was whether you had identified any specific problems that had caused this instruction to be written.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period preceding this instruction, and the causes for its issuance, were not a subject of my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we go to the first paragraph? And it's a small issue but the paragraph there describes how the security and intelligence organs are to divide their tasks, and it talks about 80 per cent of their total engagement and 20 per cent of their total engagement. In your experience, how was the engagement to be quantified? What was it referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about my experiences and I will repeat just one part that is of some significance here. I was a member of the research team which was supposed to establish the status of the security system in the JNA, which preceded the drafting of the rules and the underlying idea was to find the best solutions for engagement, command and control. It was established at that time, with scientific methods, that this relationship was optimal when the security organs are engaged at about 75 per cent level in counter-intelligence. In this instruction, this percentage has been increased to 80 per cent. I understood that. We researched the tasks and problems that occur in peacetime, whereas the problems that this instruction refers to arose from the state of war. That's why the ratio had to be changed, in order to provide for the level of efficiency that was mandated by the assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, probably my fault, but 80 per cent of what? Manpower?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 80 per cent of the capacities that could be employed, and I'm speaking about those who had the authority to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look, please, at paragraph 2 briefly? And I want to look at the second half of that paragraph. So the -- there you are. And you'll see that it says, "Furthermore, all members of these organs and services are authorised by law to act and work on tasks from their field of work analogous to the authority of the members of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior state security department." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, there is one part which expressly says that the security organs have five authorities that they can exercise in their line of duty. This was regulated for in the law on the Interior of Republika Srpska, and the rules on counter-intelligence activities pursuant to an approval of the security organs and their application in accordance with the criminal law procedure. I explained that this was individual authority proven upon the presentation of an ID that is issued to individual security officers and is non-transferrable. I mentioned these authorities expressly in my report in order to specifically state the authorities of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was this an authority which extended the authority of those people who worked within the security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska? In other words, what could members of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior state security department do that a security officer within the Army of Republika Srpska couldn't?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the authorities are identical, then there could have been no difference. It reads that they hold the authorities of the organs of the interior affairs of the state security department. So those were the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were different or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer indicates that there was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You'll forgive me this comment, there doesn't, therefore, seem to be much point in putting it in the instruction, does there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Anyway, can we now go on to paragraph 4, which relates to telegrams and mail? Is that paragraph in front of you, Mr. Vuga?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The second paragraph of paragraph 4. Is the position thus that the chief of security and possibly the Chief of Staff within a brigade or other unit would be privy to security or intelligence information which was deliberately denied to the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, let us make a distinction between intelligence data and security-related data. The difference is significant and emerged on the 13th of January when these structures were separated. This means that intelligence was sent to the brigade headquarters, and security-related information was sent to the security organ. They were treated differently, apart from being separate. When it comes to information falling within the field of counter-intelligence activities of the security organ, according to the rules that I've already explained, they did not fall within the jurisdiction of the brigade command, either from the point of view of how the activities were carried out, nor in terms of the information that was conveyed and that dealt with precisely these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vuga, but can you indicate to me where in that paragraph the sort of information that's being conveyed is divided? It says, "All telegrams and mails of the members of the security and intelligence organs shall be delivered exclusively to them personally and no other organs of the command, including the commander, have the right to inspect their contents." So where is the subject matter of the communication divided in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph was in force as such until the 13th of January, 1995, whence it ceased to apply. This period was very important for me to see how the security organs worked. The rest was in terms of the establishment quite self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on to paragraph 5, please? Again, the second paragraph of that, about personnel policy. And firstly, can you explain to me what you understand to mean by the phrase, "Members of these organs"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of these organs meant that these were senior officers and individuals who were admitted into the organs mentioned herein under special criteria and posted to the establishment posts at which they were supposed to carry out their duties in accordance with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we go down two paragraphs, please, to the fourth paragraph of that section, "Unit and institution commanders may pronounce stimulative measures, punishment and other measures for members of these organs only with obligatory consultation of the first superiors in the service." Who is the first superior in the service, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first superior in the service is establishment-wise, designated upon his appointment into the service. In the Zvornik Brigade, that was Drago Nikolic for Milorad Trbic; and for Drago Nikolic, that was the professional organ, Vujadin Popovic, chief of the security department of the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So according to your understanding of this provision, in this instruction, what could a brigade commander do to a member of the security service of his own initiative by way of stimulative measures or punishment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, the brigade commander could look at the entire work of the security organs and, having assessed that, he could pronounce an incentive. In that process, he was assisted by the professional organ, and he provided Drago Nikolic with the sufficient information that would enable him to decide whether to issue incentives or other measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, probably my fault, but a brigade commander could not directly punish his chief of security without obligatory consultation of the corps chief of security, could he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the brigade commander is the individual who assesses the entirety of the work of his organs. According to that ratio of engagement, the 20 per cent should be quite familiar to him, whereas the 80 per cent, as prescribed, meant that he had to follow-up on the line of engagement. It's in that area that I see the answer to the question as to what he could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you the same question. Look at that paragraph again, Mr. Vuga. Where is the type of work that it refers to divided? This relates to the entire performance of his task, doesn't it, if you read that instruction properly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit puzzled now. I'd like -- I should like to understand this fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, please take the time to read paragraph 5, and in particular, tell me if you can see in that paragraph which relates to the unit commander's power to pronounce stimulative measures or punishment, any distinction between counter-intelligence and other work.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other type of activity or task can be compared to counter-intelligence activities. I spoke about that when I dealt with secret covert activities and methodology. This is something that is not done by others, and that's why the specific nature of this work compared to others is manifested also in the way these tasks and the personnel involved are managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 7, please. Again, in relation to the chief of security within a brigade, who is the first superior organ for security and intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is the superior officer to the security organ. So the brigade commander is the superior officer to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You are saying, are you, that your construction of this document is that the brigade commander is the first superior organ for security and intelligence affairs to the chief of security? I want to be clear that we are not confused here.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some confusion here, sir. I spoke of the superior senior officer, whereas you're referring to professional management, or professional control, and these are two separate categories that must be kept separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm only taking the words from the document, Mr. Vuga. In paragraph 7, there is a reference to the first superior organ for security and intelligence affairs. In relation to the chief of security of a brigade, who is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is this one word that hasn't been followed through. It's the control of professionalism, so control of professionalism. It mustn't be left out. So the superior officer to Drago Nikolic was Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, in terms of that control of professionalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And what do you understand by the phrase, "Monitoring the legality of work"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mentioned. What the term means is that Drago Nikolic had to consistently and, strictly speaking, adhere to the regulations and laws governing his counter-intelligence activity, in particular in terms of covert information. In exercising that, there was no arbitrariness. He had to move within the limits prescribed by the law, and never go beyond that. He could not exercise his independence or creativity

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, and I've asked you this question twice before Mr. Vuga, where in paragraph 7 do you see any distinction between counter-intelligence work and any other sort of work that a member of a security organ might have carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the term of specialty or professionalism has to do strictly with the duties of the security organ in particular counter-intelligence activities. That was the job. The rest was the activities where other persons were the ones who were responsible for the activities and the security officers were participants in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now you've referred earlier in your evidence today to the principle of unity of command. Would you agree that within that principle, the only person who could warn a brigade commander about his conduct was his immediate superior, the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notion of warning, as you use it, is unclear to me. Warning as a disciplinary measure is one thing, and alerting somebody to a problem in order to overcome it is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a fair point, Mr. Vuga. I mean warning as a disciplinary measure. The only person who could warn a brigade commander as a disciplinary measure, if there was truly unity of command, was the corps commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could we have P176 into e-court, please? Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Take your time and have a look at it then, would you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a document addressed to the commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 72, line 17, the answer from Mr. Vuga was not correctly entered. He answered in the affirmative as having seen the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a warning of a disciplinary type to the commander of the 503rd Motorised Brigade, from whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in order for the warning to be of a disciplinary nature, we would have to find in the dossier of this commander the same warning as a disciplinary measure. This is merely a document which alerts to the fact that a violation of the regulations was committed and it's a reprimand stating that this should not happen again. The disciplinary measures are entered into the personnel file so that they can be tracked down and so that a record can be kept of the individual against whom the disciplinary measures were applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you go on like this, Colonel, you're going to be here forever. The question was a very simple one. Basically, who is issuing this warning or warning? Who is the person issuing this warning? That was the question. And if you look at the document, there is Major -- maybe Momcilo Pajic. Who is he? Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the obligation to distinguish between the warning and a proper disciplinary measure because this is now being lumped together with disciplinary measures and it is not a disciplinary measure. That's number 1. Number 2, the warning is in accordance with item 25 of the rules of service of the security organs and relates to the violation of the confidentiality of protected documents. The powers were overstepped by the officer involved, and the officer is being warned about this fact and the fact that it should not be done again. So it's not a disciplinary measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've still not answered the question. The question was: Who is this person who is signing and sending out this document? Who is he? Major Pajic, who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Major Pajic is the representative of the security organ of the superior command, of the command superior to the individual to whom the warning is addressed. He acts on behalf of the chief of the security organ of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And could you look at paragraph 1? And in particular the last sentence, and explain to me how it is consistent with a system of unity of command that a brigade commander provides a declaration on keeping secrets to his own assistant?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command is based on the application of regulations and laws which the commander is authorised to apply. There has been a violation of regulations here in the part stated herein, and as a result of the violation of powers that were vested with the commander, item 25 of the rules of service provides for an intervention to be made in such a situation. The commander's powers were overstepped in this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to move on to another document now, which is P3033, please. You've seen this before. This is the order relating to the plot called Judas, concerning the apparent plan to assassinate General Mladic or General Tolimir. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not "or," it's "and" General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you agree that this is one of those communications that is sent in such a way that the brigade commander would not see that document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document could not have been seen by anyone other than the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's obviously a very important order; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order. It has the nature of a professional action led by the security administration and approved by the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to split hairs but we will go to the body of the order. "In this respect, take the following measures during visits by these persons," et cetera, "take measures for physical security and counter-intelligence security." Taking measures for physical security of a visiting general would have been pretty much routine security work, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the application of measures in order to provide immediate security and the broader security, or the so-called security in the depth. How complex that job would be would be dictated by the location where it is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And paragraph 2, "Inform all security orders in your unit of the ordered assassination on a need-to-know basis in order to collect information related to this case." I'd like to ask you your expert opinion on this. Let us just suppose for one minute that General Mladic or General Tolimir or both of them had gone to the area of a brigade and had actually been assassinated through a lack of proper security. Given that the brigade commander never saw this instruction or order, what responsibility would he have borne for that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although your question is very hypothetical, the brigade commander would not have dealt with issues like this. These issues are beyond the scope of his methodology of work, of his powers, and everything was done to prevent the hypothetical situation that you portrayed. Everything was done in order to prevent such a murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But do you agree that he had no responsibility for what the recipients of this document were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This arises from the document. The document is limited to the security organs. Those who were not privy, who did not act upon it, could not bear any responsibility for anything that is contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this is typical of many of the orders or instructions or professional commands which a security organ in a brigade would have received without the knowledge of the brigade commander, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to omit that term "command." There is no way you can fit the term in here in any way. Those are professional instructions, to provide people with information, to carry out their tasks to the best of their abilities and knowledge, within the instructions provided to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have much more, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very, very little. But probably too much to ask you to sit on because Mr. McCloskey has got to go anyway. I don't mean to leave, he's got to cross-examine the witness yet. So I'll probably have five or ten minutes on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we will give you a rest, Colonel Vuga. We will continue on Monday at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
